elements.quote: We searched PubMed, Scopus, APA PsycInfo, and eight peer-reviewed journals to identify cancer-related studies that used system dynamics modeling. A dual review process was used to determine eligibility.
elements.reason: The abstract describes systematic-search and eligibility procedures, but it does not explicitly identify the report as a “systematic review.”

elements.quote: System dynamics modeling, which consists of diagramming and simulation approaches for understanding and managing such complexity, is being increasingly applied to cancer prevention and control, but the breadth, characteristics, and quality of these studies is not known.
elements.reason: This statement provides the main objective/review question about what is not known (breadth, characteristics, and quality).
The abstract does not specify the main inclusion and exclusion criteria.

elements.quote: We searched PubMed, Scopus, APA PsycInfo, and eight peer-reviewed journals to identify cancer-related studies that used system dynamics modeling.
elements.reason: Information sources are named, but the abstract does not report when each source was last searched.

elements.quote: Included studies were assessed using quality criteria adapted from prior literature and mapped onto the cancer control continuum.
elements.reason: The abstract describes a quality assessment, but it does not clearly specify methods used to assess risk of bias.

elements.quote: Characteristics of studies and models were abstracted and qualitatively synthesized.
elements.reason: The abstract states how results were presented/synthesized (qualitative synthesis of characteristics).

elements.quote: 32 studies met our inclusion criteria.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (32), but it does not report the total number of participants.

elements.quote: A mix of simulation and diagramming approaches were used to address diverse topics, including chemotherapy treatments (16%), interventions to reduce tobacco or e-cigarettes use (16%), and cancer risk from environmental contamination (13%). Models spanned all focus areas of the cancer control continuum, with treatment (44%), prevention (34%), and detection (31%) being the most common. The quality assessment of studies was low, particularly for simulation approaches.
elements.reason: The abstract provides results/statistics about study characteristics and quality, but it does not clearly present results for “main outcomes” in the conventional PRISMA sense (including the number of included studies and participants per outcome).
No meta-analysis is described in the available abstract evidence, so summary estimates with confidence/credible intervals are not applicable.
The abstract does not describe comparisons between groups with effect direction/favored group.

elements.quote: The quality assessment of studies was low, particularly for simulation approaches. Involvement of participants, description of model development processes, and proper calibration and validation of models showed the greatest room for improvement. Prior efforts have been hampered by a lack of rigor and transparency regarding model development and testing.
elements.reason: The abstract summarizes important limitations of the included evidence (low quality; shortcomings in participant involvement and validation/calibration; lack of rigor/transparency).

elements.quote: System dynamics modeling can illustrate complex interactions and help identify potential interventions across the cancer control continuum. ... Supportive infrastructure for increasing awareness, accessibility, and further development of best practices of system dynamics for multidisciplinary cancer research is needed.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an interpretation of results and implications for future work/infrastructure needs.

elements.quote: Funding: This project was supported by the Oregon Health & Science University Knight Cancer Institute National Cancer Institute Cancer Center Support Grant P30CA069533 (https://www.ohsu. edu/knight-cancer-institute); awarded to EK, MD, and MS. This project was also supported by the National Cancer Institute of the National Institutes of Health under Award Number UH3CA244298 (https://www.cancer.gov/research); awarded to RESEARCHARTICLE
elements.reason: The abstract includes the primary funding sources and award identifiers.
The abstract evidence provided does not report a register name and registration number.

elements.quote: Although system dynamics modeling has been utilized in various aspects of public health since the 1970s, past reviews in this field have noted a significant increase in their use since the early 2000s, especially in areas focused on chronic or non-communicable diseases [24, 25]. The extent to which system dynamics modeling has been applied specifically to cancer prevention and control has not been studied.
elements.reason: The introduction describes the existing use of system dynamics and explicitly states the knowledge gap: its extent in cancer prevention and control has not been studied.

elements.quote: Standard bench and clinical research approaches alone are not well suited to account for this complexity, as most cancer control interventions often focus on explicit, often linear health outcomes of a specific, well-defined population [1, 8, 9]. To overcome persistent barriers to providing high-quality, equitable care, approaches are needed to address this complexity and provide guidance for successful intervention.
elements.reason: The manuscript explains why a review is needed by linking the rationale to the complexity of cancer and the inadequacy of standard approaches, concluding that approaches are needed to guide successful intervention.

The retrieved evidence does not describe the need for a current review in relation to existing similar systematic reviews (e.g., identifying previous reviews, updates, replications, or citations specific to comparable systematic reviews).
The review rationale presented in the retrieved evidence does not describe an intervention effect, and there is no information about a proposed mechanism of action of an intervention.
The retrieved evidence does not provide a logic model to show hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes in a delivery context.

elements.quote: Cancer prevention and control requires consideration of complex interactions between multilevel factors. System dynamics modeling, which consists of diagramming and simulation approaches for understanding and managing such complexity, is being increasingly applied to cancer prevention and control, but the breadth, characteristics, and quality of these studies is not known.
elements.reason: The abstract states the overall purpose (unknown breadth/characteristics/quality), but the evidence does not show that review objectives/questions are explicitly stated using a relevant question-formulation framework.

elements.quote: The study was not registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) as it was a methods review and did not assess health outcomes.
elements.reason: This review is described as a methods review that did not assess health outcomes, so planned intervention comparisons using PICO (or variant) are not applicable based on the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Included articles: 1) were published in peer-reviewed journals; 2) were written in English; 3) used system dynamics modeling (i.e., causal-loop diagramming, stock-and-flow diagramming, or computational system dynamics modeling); 4) pertained to cancer prevention or control; and 4) were published within the last 10 years.
elements.reason: The review specifies several study characteristics used for eligibility (peer-reviewed, English, system dynamics modeling type, cancer prevention/control, and last 10 years), but the evidence does not specify all requested components (e.g., eligible study designs, settings, and follow-up requirements, nor an explicit question-framework breakdown).

elements.quote: Included articles: 1) were published in peer-reviewed journals; 2) were written in English; ... and 4) were published within the last 10 years.
elements.reason: Language (English) and a dissemination/publication time restriction (within the last 10 years) are specified, but the evidence does not clearly state other report-characteristics elements such as publication/report status beyond being peer-reviewed (e.g., whether preprints/reports were included or excluded).

The provided evidence does not describe a distinction between exclusions due to outcomes not being measured versus outcomes results not being reported; no such outcome-reporting exclusion categories are shown.
The evidence does not specify how studies were grouped for syntheses or how those groups were linked to comparisons defined in the review objectives.

elements.quote: In bounding our review to studies published in the last 10 years, we excluded older studies that could have contributed to this synthesis. We also excluded studies related to topics such as nutrition and physical activity if they did not include cancer in their models or research aims. While we feel this narrowed criteria was helpful in maintaining focus... Due to our focus on cancer prevention and control, we also excluded studies that were solely related to cancer pathogenesis;
elements.reason: Rationales are provided for notable eligibility restrictions (e.g., limiting to the last 10 years and excluding tangential topics and solely pathogenesis-focused studies).

elements.quote: Based on our application of the quality criteria outlined in Table 1, the overall quality of included studies was found to be low. The remaining 28 (88%) studies had missing or minimal components required by the quality criteria (i.e., scored 0-1 on at least one criterion).

elements.quote: To our knowledge, this was the first study to systematically review prior applications of system dynamics modeling across the cancer control continuum. In their review of system dynamics models pertaining to public health and medicine, Darabi and Hosseinichimeh [17] identified a handful of studies using system dynamics modeling to replicate clinical trials and simulate different interventions related to cancer, noting that this area is 'generally underexplored' and would likely benefit from further development of models for cancer screening and treatment. Similar to the findings of our paper, this review found that only a fraction of disease-related modeling studies published their model equations and methodology for development.
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly compares the review’s findings with other relevant literature (e.g., Darabi and Hosseinichimeh [17] and other scoping/review studies), interpreting results in that broader evidence context.

elements.quote:
This study has several limitations. In bounding our review to studies published in the last 10 years, we excluded older studies that could have contributed to this synthesis.

We also excluded studies related to topics such as nutrition and physical activity if they did not include cancer in their models or research aims.

Our understanding of the applications of modeling covered in the included studies was also limited by the descriptions included in the articles themselves, which were shaped by journal audience.

Our quality ratings, therefore, reflected both modeling and reporting.

Finally, the diversity of model purposes, types, and applications presented a challenge to adapting the quality assessment criteria.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly discusses multiple limitations of the evidence included in the review (e.g., restricted timeframe, excluded adjacent topics, limited descriptions in included articles, quality ratings reflecting reporting, and diversity affecting quality assessment criteria).
